subject: science
angle: While terrestrial insect biomass and abundance show significant declines, freshwater insect abundance has actually increased, and the drivers of these trends vary by habitat and region.
title: The Shifting Insect Balance

hooks.text: You think insects are dying everywhere, but some are thriving.
Your local environment is changing the life around you.
A silent garden in the middle of July.
A 76% decline in flying insect biomass.

reveal.headline: Terrestrial insects are dying while freshwater insects increase.
reveal.body: Evidence shows a complex picture where land-based insects are declining while those in water show an opposite trend.

explain.headline: The drivers of these trends vary by habitat.
explain.body: Nutrient enrichment reduces land and underground arthropods. However, nutrient additions have stronger negative effects on specific aquatic insects like mayflies and stoneflies.

matters.headline: The balance of our ecosystems is shifting.
matters.body: That may be why the birds you see depend on a shrinking food supply for their reproductive success and health.

example.headline: A backyard garden in the heat of mid-summer.
example.body: You sit outside and notice the air feels heavier and the usual hum of life has gone quiet.

question.headline: What happens when the humming stops?

stat.label: seasonal decline of flying insect biomass in German protected areas

claims.text: Flying insect biomass in protected areas in Germany declined by 76% seasonally and 82% in mid-summer over 27 years.
claims.quote: Our analysis estimates a seasonal decline of 76%, and mid-summer decline of 82% in flying insect biomass over the 27 years of study.

claims.text: Nutrient enrichment of nitrogen and phosphorus reduces the abundance of both above-ground and below-ground arthropods.
claims.quote: N + P enrichment reduced the abundance of above-ground and below-ground arthropods, suggesting that a similar mechanism driving arthropod community change is acting on both groups.

claims.text: Biological effects of non-thermal electromagnetic fields on insects are clearly proven in the laboratory, but only partly in the field.
claims.quote: Biological effects of non-thermal EMF on insects are clearly proven in the laboratory, but only partly in the field, thus the wider ecological implications are still unknown.

claims.text: Terrestrial insect abundance declined by an average of ~9% per decade, while freshwater insect abundance increased by ~11% per decade.
claims.quote: an average decline of terrestrial insect abundance by ~9% per decade and an increase of freshwater insect abundance by ~11% per decade.

claims.text: Nutrient additions have stronger negative effects on aquatic insects considered more sensitive to physical-chemical changes, such as Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera.
claims.quote: the negative effects of nutrient additions are stronger for aquatic insects that are considered more sensitive to changes in physical-chemical parameters in their environments, Ephemeroptera, Plecoptera, and Trichoptera (EPT), compared with other aquatic insects.

claims.text: Food availability is a limiting factor for breeding songbirds, with a strong positive effect on reproductive success and a moderate positive effect on chick body condition.
claims.quote: We found a moderate positive effect of food availability on chick body condition and a strong positive effect on reproductive success. Our results demonstrate that food is generally a limiting factor for breeding songbirds.

verdict: The evidence shows a complex picture where terrestrial insects are declining significantly in biomass and abundance, but freshwater insects are showing an opposite trend.
caveat: The findings are highly dependent on the specific environment, such as the distinction between terrestrial and freshwater habitats or protected versus unprotected areas.
caption:
The world is losing its insects in specific ways. 

Research shows that while terrestrial insects are declining significantly, freshwater insect abundance has actually increased. These trends are highly dependent on the specific environment. 

What do you notice about the insects in your own backyard?
